name: Tasty Cookie
description: Oh, no! The coronavirus has caught you, and now you're sitting in a dark cellar, with tied legs (but not hands). You have a delicious cookie, a laptop in front of you, and your ideal development environment is open. The coronavirus convinces you to solve the following problem. You are given two arrays $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ of size $$$n$$$. You can do operations of two types with array $$$A$$$: Reverse array $$$A$$$. That is the array $$$[A_1,\ A_2,\ \ldots,\ A_n]$$$ transformes into $$$[A_n,\ A_{n-1},\ \ldots,\ A_1]$$$. Replace $$$A$$$ with an array of its prefix sums. That is, the array $$$[A_1,\ A_2,\ \ldots,\ A_n]$$$ goes to $$$[A_1,\ (A_1+A_2),\ \ldots,\ (A_1+A_2+\ldots+A_n)]$$$. You need to understand if you can get an array $$$B$$$ from the array $$$A$$$. If it is possible, you will have to restore the order of these operations by minimizing the number of operations of the second type. Fortunately, the coronavirus is good today, so he has allowed you not to restore actions if the minimum number of second type operations is more than $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$. But coronavirus resents you, so if you restore the answer, the total number of operations should not exceed $$$5\cdot 10^5$$$. Solve this problem and get the cookie, or the coronavirus will extend the quarantine for five years and make the whole economy collapse!
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1\le n \le 2\cdot 10^5$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$$$ ($$$1 \le A_i \le 10 ^ {12}$$$). The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n$$$ ($$$1 \le B_i \le 10 ^ {12}$$$).
output_specification: If you cannot get $$$B$$$ from the $$$A$$$ array, print " IMPOSSIBLE " (without quotes) on a single line. If the minimum number of operations of the second type exceeds $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$, print " BIG " (without quotes). In the second line print the number of operations of the second type, that needs to be applied to get array $$$B$$$ from $$$A$$$. Otherwise, in the first line print " SMALL " (without quotes). In the second line print the total number of operations of the first and second types $$$m \le 5\cdot 10^5$$$ (it is guaranteed that in this case there is such a sequence of actions). In the third line print a line of length $$$m$$$, consisting of characters ' R "and ' P ' (without quotes). The $$$i$$$-th character should be ' R ', if the $$$i$$$-th action is of the first type, and should be ' P ', otherwise. If there are several such sequences, you can print any of them. You can print each character in the uppercase or in the lowercase.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1358F — Tasty Cookie [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
